meters.label: Password hits stopped by a second factor (of 216)

frames.narration: A list of 20,000 email and password pairs leaked from another site. 2,000 of the emails are customers here, and 10% of those people reuse the password.
The botnet replays the pairs, one try per account, from 5,000 addresses. No account is tried twice, and no address more than a few times. 216 pairs are still correct.

A limit of 20 failures per address and 5 per account does nothing: no counter fills up. Against only 20 addresses the per-address limit would have cut the hits to 6, which is why attackers use a botnet.

A breached-password check looks at the credential itself. If 70% of leaked passwords are known, 150 of the hits are caught and a reset is forced. The hits fall to 66, whatever addresses the attacker uses.
Now a second factor, with half the users enrolled. A correct leaked password alone no longer gets in for enrolled users. An authenticator app stops 112 of the 216 hits.

Not every factor holds the same way. Tap-to-approve push stops only 73: the attacker sends prompts until a tired owner taps yes. Number matching, or a passkey, brings it back to 112. With a live phishing page, codes can be relayed; a passkey cannot.
Even with everyone on a passkey, 57 accounts fall through account recovery: the email link skips the second factor, and those owners' email passwords were in the leak too.
Recovery that needs the same strength of proof closes the back door: with a passkey for everyone and a recovery link plus the second factor, 0 accounts are taken over.
